column11: two published figures and a census count, because no source gives paediatric ANCA-associated vasculitis as one number. (1) Paediatric granulomatosis with polyangiitis prevalence: Panupattanapong S, Stwalley DL, White AJ, Olsen MA, French AR, Hartman ME, 'Epidemiology and Outcomes of Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis in Pediatric and Working-Age Adult Populations In the United States: Analysis of a Large National Claims Database', Arthritis Rheumatol 2018;70(12):2067-2076 (doi 10.1002/art.40577, PMID 29806148, PMC6258356), MarketScan commercial claims 2006 to 2014: 'The prevalence of GPA was 3.4 cases per million person-years in children and 30.5 cases per million person-years in adults less than 65 years of age', from 214 paediatric cases over 62,419,872 child person-years. (2) The US population aged 6 to 17 at 2024-07-01, 50,652,870, summed over single years of age 6 to 17 for both sexes from US Census Bureau Vintage 2024 National Population Estimates, nc-est2024-agesex-res.csv; the file's own total of 340,110,988 matches the published US total. 3.4e-6 x 50,652,870 = 172 children with GPA. (3) The granulomatosis with polyangiitis share of paediatric ANCA-associated vasculitis, to widen GPA to the label's two diseases: Cabral DA, Canter DL, Muscal E et al. for the ARChiVe Investigators Network within the PedVas Initiative, 'Comparing Presenting Clinical Features in 48 Children With Microscopic Polyangiitis to 183 Children Who Have Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis (Wegener's): An ARChiVe Cohort Study', Arthritis Rheumatol 2016;68(10):2514-26 (doi 10.1002/art.39729, PMID 27111558): 'In total, 231 of 440 patients (64% female) fulfilled the classification criteria for either MPA (n = 48) or GPA (n = 183)', so GPA is 183/231 = 79.22%. 172 / 0.79221 = 217
column12: THREE WEAKNESSES AND THE SECOND IS SERIOUS. (a) The prevalence source is commercial claims, so Medicaid and uninsured children are not in it, and it is GPA only. (b) THE PREVALENCE AND INCIDENCE ROWS CANNOT BOTH BE RIGHT. The paper states its prevalence in 'per million person-years', its own wording, which is not a point prevalence; against the incidence row below it implies an average disease duration under two years, which is wrong for a chronic relapsing disease. Taken together the two rows understate the prevalent pool, probably by a large multiple. I wrote both as published rather than adjusting either, because any correction would need a duration or a mortality rate and neither is stated. (c) The 79.22% GPA share is of the 231 children ARChiVe could classify out of 440 recruited, so 209 unclassifiable children are outside the denominator. The share is corroborated at 81% in a different ARChiVe cohort: Gagne SJ, Sivaraman V, Bosman ES et al., Arthritis Care Res (Hoboken) 2025;77(4):504-512 (doi 10.1002/acr.25455, PMID 39467015, PMC11931354), 104 children given rituximab or cyclophosphamide induction, 'The majority had a diagnosis of GPA (81%)'. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is correctly outside this pool: NCT06321601 excludes it and the Tavneos label covers only GPA and MPA

column11: the same chain as the prevalence row above, on the same paper's incidence figure: 'The estimated incidence rate of GPA was 1.8 cases per 1,000,000 person-years in children and 12.8 cases per 1,000,000 person-years in working-age adults' (Panupattanapong 2018, 94 incident paediatric cases over 52,830,433 child person-years, 95% CI 1.4 to 2.2). 1.8e-6 x 50,652,870 = 91 children a year with GPA, / 0.79221 = 115 with ANCA-associated vasculitis
column12: the rate is measured across ages 2 to 17 and applied to the 6 to 17 population the trial enrols, which understates slightly on its face and barely in fact: the same paper reports 'The majority of pediatric patients (79.8%) were 12-18 years of age at diagnosis', so almost none of the disease sits below age 6. Read this row against the prevalence note above before using either

column11: the share on a cyclophosphamide-containing induction regimen, which is the regimen NCT06321601 requires: its title is 'Avacopan in Combination With a Rituximab or a Cyclophosphamide-containing Regimen'. Cabral DA et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2016;68(10):2514-26 (the paper cited on the prevalence row): 'Similar proportions of patients with MPA and those with GPA received combination therapy with corticosteroids plus cyclophosphamide (69% and 78%, respectively) or both drugs in combination with plasmapheresis (19% and 22%, respectively).' Weighted by the same paper's own disease split, 48 MPA and 183 GPA: (48/231) x 0.69 + (183/231) x 0.78 = 0.761299, about 165 children
column12: IT ERRS LOW, AND KNOWINGLY. The trial admits a rituximab-containing regimen as well as a cyclophosphamide-containing one, and this row counts only the cyclophosphamide arm. Cabral gives rituximab only inside a range, 'Other treatments administered, ranging in decreasing frequency from 13% to 3%, were rituximab, methotrexate, azathioprine, and mycophenolate mofetil', which is not a number, so no rituximab share is added. The split in the induction-treated population is far more even in the later ARChiVe cohort: Gagne SJ et al. 2025, 104 children, '45 patients (43%) received RTX, 48 patients (46%) received CYC, and 11 patients (11%) received a combination of RTX and CYC'. That paper gives no screened denominator, so it cannot replace the share, only show that it is low. NOT CUT, for want of published shares, and these run the other way: the trial requires 'At least 1 PVAS major item, at least 3 PVAS nonmajor items, or atleast the 2 renal items of proteinuria and hematuria', an eGFR of at least 15, a body weight of at least 15 kg, and excludes dialysis or plasmapheresis within 14 days and ventilated alveolar haemorrhage. No published share of paediatric AAV meets that bar. What is on record is that the disease is severe in most of these children: Gagne 2025 gives 'The median PVAS at diagnosis for all patients was 19 (interquartile range 16-24)' and renal disease in 87%

The published rate describes randomised Phase 3 programmes; this study is 'Open-label, Uncontrolled Single-arm' with 19 actual participants, and a paediatric extension of an adult label under PREA usually succeeds on remission rates and pharmacokinetics rather than on a controlled effect, which argues the rate is if anything low.
